questions.title: What causes the resting membrane potential
questions.question: Which of the following characterizes the resting membrane potential in nerve fibers?

options.B: Due to K+ diffusion from outside to inside the nerve fibres
options.C: Due to diffusion of intracellular protein to outside the nerve fibres
options.E: Due to unequal distribution of ions on both sides of the cell membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. The resting membrane potential of a nerve fibre is on the order of -70 to -90 mV, not 10 mV.
explanations.B: Incorrect. K+ diffuses down its concentration gradient from inside to outside the nerve fibre at rest, not the other direction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intracellular proteins are large anions that cannot cross the membrane; they help set up the ionic imbalance but do not themselves diffuse out.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump is an active, ATP-dependent process that helps maintain the ionic gradients the resting potential depends on, so the resting state is not purely passive.
explanations.E: Correct. The resting membrane potential arises because Na+, K+ and Cl- are unequally distributed across the membrane, with K+ concentrated inside and Na+ and Cl- concentrated outside. Because the membrane at rest is selectively far more permeable to K+ than to the other ions, this unequal distribution drives a net outward K+ leak that leaves the inside of the cell electrically negative relative to the outside. This ionic imbalance, maintained continuously by the Na+-K+ pump, is the fundamental basis of the resting potential.

questions.learning_objective: State that the resting membrane potential arises from the unequal distribution of ions across the nerve membrane.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Ionic Basis of the Resting Potential

questions.title: Selective permeability and the resting membrane potential
questions.question: Which one of the following does characterize the resting membrane potential in nerve fibers?

options.A: It is a passive process only
options.B: It is caused by selective permeability of the cell and unequal distribution of ions in ICF and ECF
options.C: It is due to diffusion of intracellular protein to outside the nerve fibres
options.D: It is due to K+ diffusion from outside to inside nerve fibres
options.E: Its value is normally about 10 mV

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump actively maintains the ionic gradients that the resting potential depends on, so the process is not passive alone.
explanations.B: Correct. The resting membrane potential is caused jointly by the cell membrane's selective permeability, which at rest favours K+ far more than Na+ or Cl-, and by the unequal distribution of these ions between the intracellular fluid (ICF) and extracellular fluid (ECF). Selective permeability alone would produce no potential without an ionic gradient to drive diffusion, and an ionic gradient alone would produce no potential without a membrane selectively permeable to one of the ions; the resting potential requires both together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intracellular proteins are impermeant anions that help create the ionic imbalance but do not themselves diffuse across the membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. K+ diffuses from inside to outside the nerve fibre at rest, not from outside to inside.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The resting membrane potential is roughly -70 to -90 mV in nerve fibres, not 10 mV.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the resting membrane potential jointly to the membrane's selective permeability and to the unequal ICF/ECF ion distribution.

questions.title: Measuring the resting membrane potential
questions.question: How could the resting membrane potential be measured?

options.A: Put the two electrodes inside the nerve fiber during rest
options.B: Put the two electrodes outside the nerve fiber during rest
options.C: Put the two electrodes outside the nerve fiber during stimulation of the nerve fiber by a strong stimulus
options.D: Put the two electrodes outside the nerve fiber during stimulation of the nerve fiber by a weak stimulus
options.E: Use a special voltmeter with one microelectrode inside and the second outside the nerve fibre

explanations.A: Incorrect. Placing both electrodes inside the fibre records no potential difference at all, since both tips sit on the same side of the membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Placing both electrodes outside the fibre likewise records no potential difference, since neither tip crosses the membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This arrangement records an action potential during stimulation, not the resting potential, and neither electrode is inside the cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This arrangement records a subthreshold local response at best, not the resting potential.
explanations.E: Correct. The resting membrane potential is measured with a special voltmeter connected to one microelectrode inserted inside the nerve fibre and a second, reference electrode kept outside it, with the fibre undisturbed at rest. Because the potential difference is only measured across the membrane when one electrode punctures it and the other stays on the far side, this inside-outside arrangement is required to record any transmembrane potential at all. The reading obtained this way, without any stimulus applied, is by definition the resting membrane potential.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the microelectrode arrangement (one inside, one outside the fibre) used to record the resting membrane potential.

questions.title: Ion whose small concentration change most affects the resting potential
questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a cell is most affected by even a small change in the plasma concentration of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Because resting membrane permeability to Na+ is low, a small change in plasma Na+ concentration has little effect on the resting potential.
explanations.B: Correct. The resting membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to any other ion, so the resting potential sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential predicted by the Nernst equation. Because that equilibrium potential is a logarithmic function of the K+ concentration ratio across the membrane, even a small change in plasma (extracellular) K+ concentration shifts the ratio enough to noticeably change the resting potential — which is exactly why clinical hypo- or hyperkalemia disturbs excitable-tissue function. No other ion's plasma concentration has this outsized effect at rest, precisely because the membrane is not nearly as permeable to them.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Resting Cl- permeability, while present, does not dominate the resting potential the way K+ permeability does.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Resting Ca2+ permeability is low, so small plasma Ca2+ changes have little direct effect on the resting membrane potential itself, even though Ca2+ affects the threshold for firing.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why the resting membrane potential is exquisitely sensitive to small changes in plasma K+ concentration.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > K+ Permeability Dominance at Rest

questions.title: Highest resting membrane permeability
questions.question: Which ion has the highest permeability at rest?

explanations.A: Correct. At rest, the nerve fibre membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to any other ion, because far more of the membrane's resting (leak) channels are potassium-selective than sodium-, chloride- or calcium-selective. This high resting K+ permeability is why the resting potential sits so close to the K+ equilibrium potential predicted by the Nernst equation, and it holds regardless of which other ion is compared against it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Resting Na+ permeability is low; it rises sharply only once voltage-gated Na+ channels open during depolarization.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Resting Cl- permeability, while present in many cells, does not exceed resting K+ permeability in nerve fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Resting Ca2+ permeability is low compared with resting K+ permeability.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Mg2+ is not a major determinant of resting membrane permeability in nerve fibres.

questions.learning_objective: Name K+ as the ion with the highest membrane permeability at rest.

questions.title: Definition of equilibrium potential
questions.question: In equilibrium potential:

options.C: The diffusion force equals the repulsion force, and no diffusion occurs
options.D: The diffusion of ions occurs through voltage-gated ion channels
options.E: Ions diffuse against their concentration gradient

explanations.A: Incorrect. The K+ equilibrium potential is about -94 mV (approximately -90 mV in round numbers), not +60 mV — that value belongs to Na+.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Na+ equilibrium potential is about +61 mV, not -90 mV — the values for Na+ and K+ have been swapped in this option.
explanations.C: Correct. At an ion's equilibrium potential, the electrical force pulling the ion back (the repulsion/attraction generated by the charge separation already present) exactly balances the chemical force driving it to diffuse down its concentration gradient. Because these two opposing forces are equal and opposite at that specific voltage, there is no further net diffusion of the ion across the membrane, even though individual ions continue to move in both directions. This is precisely what the Nernst equation calculates for a given ion and concentration gradient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reaching equilibrium potential does not require voltage-gated channels specifically; it is a property of any membrane permeable to the ion, including via resting leak channels.
explanations.E: Incorrect. At equilibrium, net diffusion stops entirely; ions do not diffuse against their concentration gradient at equilibrium.

questions.learning_objective: Define equilibrium potential as the voltage at which an ion's chemical (diffusion) and electrical (repulsion) forces are equal and opposite.

questions.title: Direction of Na+-K+ pump transport
questions.question: Which of the following is the action of the sodium-potassium pump in maintaining the resting membrane potential (RMP) of neurons?

options.A: Transferring Na+ and K+ into the cell
options.B: Transferring Na+ and K+ out of the cell
options.C: Transferring Na+ into the cell and K+ out of the cell
options.D: Transferring Na+ out of the cell and K+ into the cell
options.E: Transferring Na+ and K+ into the cell and H+ out of the cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is the opposite of both ions' true pumped direction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. K+ is pumped into, not out of, the cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses both ions' true pumped direction — the pump moves Na+ out and K+ in, not the reverse.
explanations.D: Correct. The Na+-K+ pump is an antiport that uses the energy of ATP hydrolysis to move Na+ out of the cell and K+ into the cell, both against their electrochemical gradients — specifically, three Na+ ions out for every two K+ ions in. This active, continuous transport is what maintains the high intracellular K+ and high extracellular Na+ concentrations on which the resting membrane potential ultimately depends. Without it, the ionic gradients that set up the resting potential would gradually run down.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump does not transport H+; it exchanges Na+ and K+ only.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Na+-K+ pump moves Na+ out of and K+ into the cell to maintain the resting potential's ionic gradients.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Na+-K+ Pump and Active Transport

questions.title: Typical value of the neuronal resting membrane potential
questions.question: What is the resting membrane potential in a neuron?

explanations.A: Correct. The typical resting membrane potential of a medium-sized neuron is about -70 mV, with the inside of the cell negative relative to the outside. This value reflects the membrane's dominant resting permeability to K+ together with the small additional contribution of the electrogenic Na+-K+ pump. Larger nerve and skeletal muscle fibres can reach about -90 mV, but -70 mV is the standard quoted value for a typical neuron.
explanations.B: Incorrect. -70 V is a thousand times too large — membrane potentials are measured in millivolts, not volts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A positive 100 mV has both the wrong sign and the wrong magnitude for the resting state.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A positive 70 mV has the wrong sign — the inside of a resting neuron is negative, not positive, relative to the outside.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A positive 70 V has both the wrong sign and is off by a factor of a thousand in magnitude.

questions.learning_objective: State the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron as about -70 mV.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Definition and Magnitude of RMP

questions.title: Definition of membrane potential
questions.question: Membrane potential is the difference in electrical charge between which of the following?

options.B: The inside and outside of the cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. Potassium and sodium are two of the ions whose unequal distribution helps generate the potential, but the potential itself is not defined as a difference between two ion species.
explanations.B: Correct. Membrane potential is, by definition, the electrical potential difference measured across the cell membrane — that is, between the inside (intracellular) and outside (extracellular) surfaces of the membrane. It is this transmembrane voltage, generated by the unequal distribution and selective permeability of ions, that is recorded when one electrode is placed inside the cell and a reference electrode outside it. All specific forms of membrane potential — resting, action and local potentials — are instances of this same inside-versus-outside electrical difference.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phosphoric acid and glycolipids are membrane chemical constituents, not the basis of the electrical potential definition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Resting and action potentials are two states of the membrane potential over time, not the two sides across which it is measured.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sodium and chloride are two of the ions involved in generating the potential, not the two sides across which it is defined.

questions.learning_objective: Define membrane potential as the electrical potential difference between the inside and outside of the cell.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Definition and Magnitude of RMP

questions.title: Na+-K+ pump activity at rest
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the Na+-K+ pump?

options.A: It pumps 2 Na+ ions outside, and 3 K+ ions inside
options.B: It maintains a high concentration of Na+ inside and K+ outside the nerve
options.C: It prevents Cl- ions from entering the nerve cells
options.D: It pumps K+ ions from inside to outside

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stoichiometry is reversed and swapped — the pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, not 2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pump maintains the opposite arrangement: high Na+ outside and high K+ inside the nerve fibre, not high Na+ inside and K+ outside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Na+-K+ pump does not transport Cl-; it exchanges Na+ and K+ only.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pump moves K+ from outside to inside the cell, the opposite direction stated here.
explanations.E: Correct. The Na+-K+ pump is continuously active, including at rest, steadily extruding Na+ and importing K+ against their electrochemical gradients using ATP. This ongoing activity at rest is exactly what maintains the resting ionic gradients against the constant passive leak of Na+ in and K+ out through resting channels. Without this continuous resting activity, the gradients underlying the resting membrane potential would gradually dissipate.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Na+-K+ pump is continuously active, including during rest, to maintain the resting ionic gradients.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Na+-K+ Pump and Active Transport

questions.title: Extracellular chloride concentration
questions.question: As regards ionic distribution inside and outside the nerve fibers, which of the following is TRUE?

options.A: Na+ ions are the main cations inside the nerve fibers
options.B: K+ ions are the main cations outside the nerve fibers
options.C: Na+ ion concentration is 4 mEq/L outside the nerve fiber
options.D: K+ ion concentration is 14 mEq/L outside the nerve fiber
options.E: Cl- ion concentration is about 100 mEq/L outside the nerve fiber

explanations.A: Incorrect. K+, not Na+, is the main cation inside the nerve fibre.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Na+, not K+, is the main cation outside the nerve fibre.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is roughly the intracellular K+ concentration figure, not the extracellular Na+ concentration, which is around 142 mEq/L.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is roughly the extracellular K+ concentration figure stated too low and mislabelled; extracellular K+ is closer to 4 mEq/L, not 14.
explanations.E: Correct. Extracellular chloride concentration in nerve fibres is approximately 100-120 mEq/L, far higher than the low intracellular Cl- concentration. This large outward-directed Cl- gradient, together with the membrane's Cl- permeability, contributes to the resting membrane potential alongside the dominant K+ gradient. The asymmetric distribution of Cl-, like that of Na+ and K+, is actively maintained rather than allowed to equilibrate freely.

questions.learning_objective: State the approximate extracellular chloride concentration in nerve fibres and identify which ions are the main intracellular versus extracellular cations.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Ionic Basis of the Resting Potential

questions.title: Definition of excitable tissue
questions.question: About excitable tissues, which of the following is TRUE?

options.B: Their cell membranes are in a polarization state
options.C: They include all tissue cells except those present in bones
options.D: They are present in the central and peripheral nervous systems only
options.E: There is no potential difference between the inside and outside of their cell membranes

explanations.A: Incorrect. By definition, an excitable tissue is one that CAN respond to a stimulus by generating an action potential.
explanations.B: Correct. Excitable tissues such as nerve and muscle rest in a polarized state, meaning their cell membranes maintain a stable resting potential with the inside negative relative to the outside. This polarized baseline is precisely what allows the membrane to respond to an adequate stimulus by depolarizing and generating a propagated action potential. Non-excitable cells either lack this polarized, responsive membrane or cannot generate a propagated regenerative response from it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Excitable tissues are specifically nerve and muscle (and some gland cells); most other body tissue cells are not classified as excitable, regardless of bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Excitable tissue includes muscle (skeletal, cardiac and smooth) as well as nerve, not the nervous system alone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Excitable tissues characteristically DO have a resting potential difference between the inside and outside of the membrane; this polarized state is a prerequisite for excitability, not its absence.

questions.learning_objective: State that excitable tissues rest in a polarized state, which is the basis of their ability to respond to a stimulus.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Excitability of Tissues

questions.title: Na+-K+ pump maintenance role
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about the Na+-K+ pump?

options.A: It is an example of facilitated diffusion
options.B: It does not require the input of cellular energy in the form of ATP
options.C: It moves Na+ and K+ ions along their concentration gradient
options.D: It is composed of a phospholipid located in the plasma membrane
options.E: It is necessary for the maintenance of intracellular K+ and extracellular Na+

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion carries a substance down its gradient without energy input; the Na+-K+ pump is active transport, moving ions against their gradients using ATP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pump requires ATP hydrolysis via its own ATPase activity; without ATP it cannot maintain the ionic gradients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pump moves Na+ and K+ against, not along, their concentration gradients — that is precisely why it needs energy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pump is a transmembrane protein (an alpha and a beta subunit), not a phospholipid.
explanations.E: Correct. The Na+-K+ pump is necessary for maintaining the characteristic ionic asymmetry of excitable cells: high intracellular K+ and high extracellular Na+. By continuously extruding Na+ and importing K+ against their gradients, it counteracts the constant passive leak of these ions through resting channels. This maintained asymmetry is what makes the resting membrane potential possible in the first place.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Na+-K+ pump is necessary for maintaining the characteristic high intracellular K+ and high extracellular Na+ concentrations.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Na+-K+ Pump and Active Transport

questions.title: Direction of K+ diffusion generating the resting potential
questions.question: The resting membrane potential in nerve fibers is:

options.B: Due to Na+ diffusion from outside to inside the nerve fibers
options.C: Due to diffusion of intracellular protein to outside the nerve fibers
options.E: Due to K+ diffusion from inside to outside the nerve fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. The resting membrane potential is roughly -70 to -90 mV, not -10 mV.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Na+ permeability at rest is low, so Na+ diffusion does not drive the resting potential; K+ diffusion does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intracellular proteins are impermeant and do not diffuse across the resting membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Maintaining the ionic gradients that generate the resting potential requires the active, ATP-dependent Na+-K+ pump, so the overall state is not purely passive.
explanations.E: Correct. Because the resting membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to any other ion, K+ diffuses down its concentration gradient from inside the fibre, where it is concentrated, to outside. This net outward movement of positive charge leaves the inside of the membrane electrically negative relative to the outside, which is the direct ionic basis of the resting membrane potential. The magnitude of the resulting potential sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential predicted by the Nernst equation, reflecting K+'s dominant resting permeability.

questions.learning_objective: State that the resting membrane potential is generated by K+ diffusion from inside to outside the nerve fibre.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Ionic Basis of the Resting Potential

questions.title: Ion channel selectivity
questions.question: About ion channels, which of the following is TRUE?

options.A: These channels allow only specific ions to pass while blocking others because of their size, charge, or state of hydration
options.B: Voltage-gated ion channels can be opened by combination with chemical substances
options.C: Passive channels open only when there is a difference in concentration gradient
options.D: Na+ channels allow all positively charged ions to pass through them
options.E: Chemically activated ion channels (receptors) are not gated

explanations.A: Correct. Ion channels are selective pores that allow only specific ions to cross the membrane while excluding others, and this selectivity is determined by the channel's pore size, the charge lining the pore, and the hydration state the ion must shed to pass through. This selective-filter property is what allows, for example, a voltage-gated Na+ channel to admit Na+ far more readily than K+, even though both are small cations. Selectivity of this kind underlies the whole ionic basis of membrane potentials, since different channel types create different, ion-specific permeability pathways.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Voltage-gated channels are opened by a change in membrane voltage, not by combination with a chemical substance — that description applies to chemically (ligand) gated channels instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Passive (leak) channels are typically open continuously and are not gated open only by a concentration gradient; a concentration gradient determines the direction of net flow through an already-open channel, not whether it opens.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Na+ channels are selective for Na+, not for all positively charged ions indiscriminately.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chemically activated (ligand-gated) ion channels are, by definition, gated — they open in response to binding a chemical ligand.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that ion channel selectivity depends on pore size, charge, and the ion's state of hydration.
questions.module_subject: MANS-AEP > Physiology > Resting Membrane Potential > Ion Channel Selectivity
